I will keep my system simple, intensive, and familiar: a winter wheat followed by summer maize rotation on most of my land. In Quzhou County that matches the climate, the irrigation conditions of the North China Plain, and the grain market I would trust most at my age. Since I am well educated, I would lean on improved or hybrid seed, soil testing, and tighter input control rather than farming by habit alone. I would avoid scattering my attention across too many crops. At 72, I would value reliability, mechanization, and stable yield more than chasing a complicated high-value crop.

For the winter season, I would plant winter wheat because it fits the local calendar and uses the cold season well. I would use improved seed, aim for strong early establishment, apply balanced nitrogen with enough phosphorus for rooting, and add potassium to support lodging resistance and grain filling. I would plough before wheat because I want a clean seedbed and better residue incorporation after maize. I would irrigate about three times in a normal year: once around overwintering or before freeze if moisture is short, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if needed. I would keep pesticide sprays limited but timely, mainly for aphids, rusts, or powdery mildew if pressure appears.

After wheat harvest, I would quickly shift into summer maize. That is the second half of the rotation I would rely on for total annual output. For maize I would use hybrid seed for vigor and uniformity. I would prefer rotary tillage after wheat harvest because it is fast and practical in the short turnaround window. I would put more nitrogen on maize than on wheat, keep phosphorus moderate, and maintain potassium because maize removes a lot. I would irrigate two times in a normal year, mainly around the big demand stages, and I would keep pest control focused on the actual field situation rather than routine overuse. My goal would be stable, high grain yield with manageable labor and manageable risk.
